terms.gloss: a boundary, a limit, an end; here, the date by which food should be eaten
evidence: Cic. Lael. 56: quasi terminī dīligendī (Lewis & Short)
M-O s.v. deadline: expiration date, terminus
terms.comment: Classically a boundary, and then any limit or end. Morgan–Owens gives it for an expiration date, from an early-modern use of it for the end of a truce. Its use for the date on food is modern, and ours. In speech the plain question is Quī diēs in pittaciō scrīptus est?: pittacium is Petronius’s word for the label on a jar.

phrases.latin: Quī terminus in pittaciō scrīptus est?
phrases.english: What’s the best-before date on the label?

phrases.latin: Hoc lac terminum suum praeteriit; abjice.
phrases.english: This milk is past its date; throw it away.

phrases.latin: Statim allātae sunt amphorae vitreae dīligenter gypsātae, quārum in cervīcibus pittacia erant affīxa cum hōc titulō: Falernum Opīmiānum annōrum centum.
phrases.english: At once glass jars carefully sealed with plaster were brought in, with labels fixed to their necks bearing this title: Falernian, Opimian vintage, a hundred years old.

sources: Lewis & Short: terminus · Lewis & Short: pittacium
